v.why: When edge 2->3 is empty, a conv on 1->3 supplies a missing parametric path to the output (exps 48, 92 show large gains).
If edge 1->3 is only pooling, a conv on 2->3 provides much-needed learnable capacity at the output (exps 96, 100).
Replacing a conv on 0->1 with parameter-free pooling removes capacity feeding nodes 1-3, which hurts more than replacing none/skip (exps 7, 37).
Removing a pooling edge is harmless or helpful, while removing a conv on 0->1 consistently hurts (exps 10, 14 vs 54, 59, 75).
Deleting a 3x3 conv on an output edge removes a key learnable path, unlike deleting a pool (exps 28, 46 vs 89).
Swapping a 3x3 conv for identity on 1->3 loses capacity, whereas swapping out pool or none is neutral or positive (exp 81 vs 5, 91).
Replacing a 3x3 conv on 0->2 with pooling discards the strongest op on that edge (exp 1).
Upgrading pooling to a 3x3 conv on 2->3 adds capacity, whereas upgrading an existing 1x1 conv gives little or nothing (exp 71 vs 72).
A skip in place of pooling on 0->3 restores clean gradient flow, while a skip in place of a conv removes capacity (exps 9, 42, 61 vs 8).
Removing pooling on 1->2 tends to help, while removing a conv there hurts (exps 32, 53 vs 30, 36).
